input:
The goal of this worked example is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, together with the fraction of reactant that remains after 60 min. The measured rate constant for the reaction is k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, and it was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is connected to the rate constant by the well-known relationship t1/2 = ln(2)/k, while the fraction of reactant remaining after a time t is given by exp(-k t). It is important to bear in mind that these relationships are valid for a first-order reaction only, since a reaction of any other order would follow an entirely different decay law.

Substituting the measured value into the half-life relationship gives t1/2 = ln(2)/0.023, which evaluates to 30.1 min. In a similar way, the fraction remaining after 60 min is obtained from the decay relationship as exp(-0.023 × 60), which comes out at 0.25. As a final sanity check, it is reassuring to observe that the elapsed time of 60 min is very close to twice the half-life of 30.1 min, and since each half-life reduces the amount of reactant by half, two half-lives should leave behind one quarter of the original amount, which is exactly the value of 0.25 that the calculation produced.
target:
Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction from its rate constant, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant is k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is fixed by the rate constant through t1/2 = ln(2)/k, and the fraction remaining after a time t is exp(-k t). Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law. The half-life is the time in which the amount of reactant falls to one half of the amount present at the start of the interval. The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the amount present: every interval of one half-life halves what remains. The fraction remaining is the amount still present at the stated time, divided by the amount at the start.

The half-life follows from the rate constant directly: t1/2 = ln(2)/0.023 = 30.1 min. The fraction remaining after 60 min follows from the decay relation: exp(-0.023 × 60) = 0.25.

The fraction is checked against the half-life. The elapsed time, 60 min, is close to twice the half-life of 30.1 min, and two half-lives reduce the reactant to one quarter of its initial amount. The computed fraction, 0.25, is the quarter the check requires. The fraction is dimensionless, as a ratio of two amounts in the same unit must be.
